alignments.note: Connective δέ realized by the clause-initial Now; the ASV's reordering is immaterial.
Ordinary conditional ἐάν → if (rule 72's closing clause).
Subjunctive rendered by the bare English subjunctive come.
Imperative βλέπετε → see; no subject word supplied.
ἵνα realized by the word introducing its English clause (rule 40), here that.
Inflected verb takes its English subject pronoun as a helper (rules 7, 9); head on the lexical verb be, not on he.
πρός → with; the preposition governing the phrase realizes the Greek preposition (rule 36).
Privative adverb rendered without + noun; head on fear, the noun glossing the lexeme, with without spelling only the alpha-privative (rule 84).
Inflected verb with its supplied subject pronoun; head on worketh (rule 17).
Article to the (rule 19); split from its noun under rule 26.
Bare noun, its determiner standing on the article.

Anarthrous genitive: no Greek article stands to take the supplied the, so the whole of the Lord belongs to κυρίου, the case preposition riding with it (rules 21, 51 anarthrous clause). Head on the noun.
Comparative adverb keeps its own as (rule 82).

Crasis takes both English words, the pronoun I and the καί's also, headed on the pronominal (rule 55). The elliptical comparative clause expresses no predicate of its own — ἐργάζεται is already spent on worketh — so the supplied pro-verb do rides with the subject under rule 56 rather than being marked added under rule 103. Variant SBLGNT.1CO.16.10.v010 is underdetermined with r00-base and r02 both compatible and the base carried, so no textual question arises here (rule 12).

review_notes: Every source and target ID is partitioned exactly once.
s007 headed on fear rather than without, following rule 84's unbroken corpus line for privative adverbs.
s014 keeps of the Lord whole because the projection carries no article for the Lord; had one stood, rule 21 would have given it of the.

The competing reading for s017 is marking do added under rule 103 as a resumption of the spent ἐργάζεται; rule 56's elliptical-comparative clause is why the supplied verb rides with the subject instead.
